summary: Defines the Trust Anchor Locator, a small file telling a validator where to find a trust anchor certificate and what public key to expect. It was replaced by RFC 7730.

eli5.summary: Every trust chain starts somewhere. This is a small note saying where to find the starting point and how to check it is the right one. It was later replaced by RFC 7730.

questions: what is a trust anchor locator
how does rpki use trust anchors
subtitle: A small file that tells validators where to find the root of a trusted certificate chain.

tldr.problem: In RPKI, trust anchors are self-signed certificates that define which Internet number resources an entity controls. When resources change hands, the entire certificate must be redistributed, creating operational friction.
tldr.mechanism: The Trust Anchor Locator (TAL) separates the certificate location and verification from the certificate itself, storing only an rsync URI and a public key fingerprint in a small text file.
tldr.outcome: Validators can verify trust anchors without redistributing them when their resource allocations change. RFC 7730 later replaced this format with an updated version.

facts.label: Key stability requirement
facts.value: Public key must not change across certificate reissues

today: RFC 6490 was obsoleted by RFC 7730, which updated the TAL format. RFC 6490 remains an important historical reference for RPKI trust anchor distribution.

sections.title: What RPKI and Trust Anchors Are
sections.content:
The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) uses cryptographic certificates to bind Internet number resources (like IP addresses and AS numbers) to their owners. Unlike the traditional certificate authority hierarchy on the web, RPKI trust chains start with self-signed trust anchor certificates—certificates that vouch for themselves and are accepted because an organization has decided to trust them out-of-band.

Each trust anchor certificate contains an extension listing the Internet number resources that entity controls. As resource allocations change over time, the certificate must be reissued. If validators kept just the certificate, every change would require redistribution of the new certificate to all relying parties, a painful operational process.
sections.eli5: RPKI is like a phone book that uses fingerprints instead of names to identify people. At the root, someone has to say "I trust this person and here are their phone numbers." That root certificate is the trust anchor. When the person's phone numbers change, you need a new certificate, but updating everyone is a hassle.

sections.title: The TAL Format
sections.content:
The Trust Anchor Locator is elegantly simple: a text file containing exactly two things. The first is an rsync URI that points to the location of the trust anchor certificate—for example, rsync://rpki.example.org/rpki/hedgehog/root.cer. The second, on the next line, is the Base64-encoded public key from that certificate, which lets validators verify they have the right certificate.

This two-line format decouples the location from the content. The URI never changes for a given trust anchor, so it can be distributed once out-of-band (by email, paper, or manual configuration). The certificate at that location can be reissued any number of times—when resources change, when the certificate nears expiration, or for any other reason—and validators will fetch and use the new one automatically.
sections.eli5: It is like a contract that says "Go to this address and check that the person you find there has this fingerprint." The address does not change, but the person can get a new ID card, and you still know you have the right person because the fingerprint is printed on your contract.

sections.title: Requirements for the Trust Anchor
sections.content:
The certificate at the rsync URI MUST be a self-signed X.509 certificate that conforms to the RPKI certificate profile (RFC 6487). It MUST NOT use the "inherit" form of resource extensions; instead, it MUST explicitly list the resources it claims authority over. Because the public key is baked into the TAL, it MUST remain stable: the same key is used every time the certificate is reissued, even if the resource list changes.

To keep this key secure, the RFC recommends operating the trust anchor offline. The entity should issue a subordinate CA certificate that inherits the same resources and use that online instead, reserving the offline root key for future reissuing of the trust anchor if needed. This way, if the online subordinate key is compromised, the root certificate can be revoked via its CRL without affecting the TAL itself.
sections.eli5: The certificate has to stay the same except for what is inside it. Imagine a passport: the name and ID number never change, but you can update your address inside it. The important bit is keeping the ID number—the public key—the same so nobody questions whether it is you.

sections.title: How Validators Use the TAL
sections.content:
A relying party that receives a TAL should first fetch the certificate from the rsync URI and confirm it is a valid RPKI CA certificate. Then it verifies that the public key embedded in the file matches the one in the retrieved certificate. Once these checks pass, the validator has a trust anchor it can use to verify downstream certificates and resources in the RPKI.

Because certificates can be reissued, validators should re-check the TAL each time they synchronize their local repository cache, and always before the cached certificate expires. If an entity wishes to retire a trust anchor (for example, due to key compromise), it simply removes the certificate from the rsync URI, and validators will stop accepting it.
sections.eli5: When you receive a TAL, go to the address it says, check that the certificate there matches the fingerprint in your TAL, and then you can trust anything signed by that certificate.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
Compromise of a trust anchor private key is catastrophic, since an attacker can then create false resource allocations. The TAL itself does not directly list the resources the trust anchor claims; validators must fetch the certificate and read its resource extension to know what is authoritative. This provides operational flexibility but also allows the certificate issuer to claim authority over any resource. Relying parties should have high confidence in their trust anchors, or better yet, run their own self-signed root and constrain subordinates under it.

The TAL format itself was adopted by RPKI implementors early in the design and became the de facto standard before PKIX standardized a similar TrustAnchorInfo structure. The RPKI community chose the simplicity of ASCII-encoded TALs over binary encodings.
sections.eli5: A hacker who steals the trust anchor's secret key can forge anything. So you need to really trust whoever owns the anchor. The TAL format is simple and text-based, which makes it easier to use than more complicated formats.
